summary: Astro Quest is a browser game where kids run a small research base in Gale Crater on Mars. They guide an astronaut and a fictional rover, R-1, through six science stages that follow Curiosity’s real discoveries. Every decision rests on real NASA data, fetched live whenever possible. A real coronal mass ejection from DONKI becomes a storm warning, and the child works out its arrival time from the true speed. Curiosity’s RAD measurements fill a dosimeter chart. OSDR space-biology studies turn into new base rules: exercise protects muscles, and tomatoes grow under LED light. NASA Mars Trek altitude maps and Curiosity photos drive the map-reading quizzes. Each screen shows its source and labels what is real and what is simulated, so children learn to tell fact, hypothesis and simulation apart. The game addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge with short missions that teach the trade-offs of living on Mars: energy, life support, radiation and teamwork. It runs in any browser, needs no install, and is available in Portuguese, English and Spanish.
details:
Astro Quest is a 3D base-building game set in Gale Crater. The player places a habitat, a plant dome and a comms tower, then keeps three resources balanced: Energy, Life support and Health. Messages from Earth unlock six stages that retrace Curiosity’s mission: the landing site, wheel damage, lake mudstones, drill holes, the climb up Mount Sharp, and Vera Rubin Ridge. Between stages, short missions teach one real idea each: cleaning dust off solar panels after a storm, sealing a leak against low pressure, sheltering from a solar storm, reading an altitude map, classifying rocks and growing lettuce under coloured light.

How it uses NASA data. Small serverless proxies keep the API key off the client and cache each response:

  • DONKI: live solar events and CME speed, used for the storm-arrival math.
  • Mars raw images: Curiosity’s latest photos, used as the “photo of the day” and in the final gallery.
  • OSDR: real study titles and results, used as lab predictions that become base rules.
  • OSDR RadLab: Curiosity RAD dose from September 2017, shown in the dosimeter chart.

When the network is down, the game falls back to stored real values and says so.

Why it matters. Children practise reading graphs, scales and evidence, and they see that science changes decisions. Every screen is labelled as fact or simulation, and the fictional rover R-1 is never presented as Curiosity.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, three.js (r128) for the 3D scene, Vercel serverless functions and Playwright for browser testing. Texts are in Portuguese, English and Spanish.

Design choices. Big touch targets, one action per window, text-to-speech, reduced-motion support, and an offline mode for classrooms with poor internet.
